The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. For
$0\le t\le T$, let
$(E_t,\mathcal E_t)$ be a standard-Borel state space; for $1\le t\le T$, let
$(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ be a standard-Borel observation space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]), meaning a measurable space bimeasurably
isomorphic to a Polish space. A probability kernel has probability-measure
sections and measurable evaluations as in
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Specify an initial probability
measure $\mu_0$ on $E_0$ (a measure of total mass one, as in
[[def-probability-measure]]), transition probability kernels $K_t$ from
$E_{t-1}$ to $E_t$, and observation probability kernels $G_t$ from $E_t$ to
$F_t$, for $1\le t\le T$.

The trajectory space, with the finite product sigma-algebra generated by
measurable coordinate rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), is
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
with $\mathcal Z_0=E_0$. Its finite-horizon law $P_T$ is the unique probability
law whose ordered iterated kernel integral is
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order; it
does not assert the existence of densities. Existence and uniqueness under AC
are proved in [[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]].
Every finite product trajectory space is standard Borel by
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].

The initial and transition laws specify the state evolution, while each
$G_t$ specifies the observation law given the current state in this model.
State evolution by itself therefore does not specify a joint state-observation
law. No density or time-homogeneity assumption is imposed, and no strict
stationarity assumption (shift invariance of all finite-dimensional laws) is
required ([[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]]). This is a
single law, not a parameter-indexed family. The model contract records a
proposed law and makes no claim that it adequately describes an application
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, standard-Borel spaces
$E_0,\ldots,E_T$ and $F_1,\ldots,F_T$, an initial probability measure
$\mu_0$ on $E_0$, and transition and observation probability kernels
$K_t:E_{t-1}\to E_t$ and $G_t:E_t\to F_t$ for $1\le t\le T$, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. On the interleaved finite
product space
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
there is a unique probability measure whose rectangle probabilities are the
ordered iterated kernel integrals
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order.
For $T=0$, the assertion is the initial law $\mu_0$ on $E_0$.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Assume AC. Let $X$ and $Y$ take values in nonempty standard-Borel spaces $(E,\mathcal S)$ and $(T,\mathcal T)$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. Let $L$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, everywhere a probability kernel. There is a probability kernel $K:T\to E$ such that $L(\omega,\cdot)=K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ simultaneously outside a single null set. In fact, with the stated everywhere-kernel convention, the construction below gives this equality for every $\omega$. Consequently K is a conditional law of X given Y.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times

and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by

$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish

$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional

**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel

$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

Let $K$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ given $\mathcal G$. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, the measurable function $I_f(\omega)=\int f(x)K(\omega,dx)$ satisfies

$$\int_H I_f\,dP=\int_H f(X)\,dP\qquad(H\in\mathcal G).$$

This assertion is choice-free. Under AC, it says $I_f=E[f(X)\mid\mathcal G]$ as nonnegative almost-sure classes. If $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is measurable and $E|f(X)|<\infty$, put $D=\{I_{|f|}<\infty\}$. Then $D\in\mathcal G$, $P(D)=1$, and the signed integral on $D$, extended by zero off $D$, is a real integrable conditional-expectation version of $f(X)$. Its identification with the AC-based conditional-expectation class uses AC only for that class convention.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC and a finite-horizon state-space model by standard-Borel state and
observation spaces, an initial probability measure, and transition and
observation probability kernels, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. Let $P_T$ be its finite-horizon
path law. The initial filtering kernel is $\pi_0=\mu_0$ on the singleton
empty-history space. For each $1\le t\le T$, data-indexed filtering and
predictive kernels from [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] exist. A
data-indexed finite-horizon smoothing kernel for the full state path also
exists, including when $T=0$. The claim is existence of conditional versions
only; it asserts no density, filtering recursion, uniqueness on null
observation histories, or numerical approximation.

Assume AC and a finite-horizon model as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. For each $1\le t\le T$, suppose
the observation kernel has a supplied product-measurable density
$g_t:E_t\times F_t\to[0,\infty]$ with respect to a sigma-finite measure
$\nu_t$ on $F_t$, normalized so that
$$G_t(x,B)=\int_Bg_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy),\qquad\int_{F_t}g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy)=1$$
for every state $x$ and measurable $B\subseteq F_t$.

The procedure takes the initial law $\mu_0$, transition kernels $K_t$,
observation densities $g_t$ and measures $\nu_t$ as inputs. It defines
data-indexed prediction, evidence, and filtering functions on every
observation history as follows.

1. Initialize $\pi_0$ on the singleton empty-history space by
$\pi_0(*,A)=\mu_0(A)$.

2. For $t=1,\ldots,T$, each history $h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$ and each
measurable state set $A\in\mathcal E_t$, form the predictive measure
$$\widehat\pi_t(h,A):=\int_{E_{t-1}}K_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(h,dx).$$

3. For each $y\in F_t$, calculate the evidence density
$$z_t(h,y):=\int_{E_t}g_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx).$$

4. Define the filtering measure at $(h,y)$ by
$$\pi_t(h,y,A):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ag_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)}{z_t(h,y)},&0<z_t(h,y)<\infty,\\[6pt]\widehat\pi_t(h,A),&z_t(h,y)=0\text{ or }z_t(h,y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Use $\pi_t$ as the input filtering function at the next time step.

The procedure returns $\widehat\pi_t$, $z_t$, and $\pi_t$ for every
$1\le t\le T$. It is an exact measure-valued recursion; it makes no claim
that the integrals have closed forms or can be evaluated with finite

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

Assume AC and a finite-horizon model as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. For each $1\le t\le T$, let
$\nu_t$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ and suppose the
observation kernel has a specified product-measurable density
$g_t:E_t\times F_t\to[0,\infty]$ with respect to $\mathcal E_t\otimes\mathcal F_t$:
$$G_t(x,B)=\int_B g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy),\qquad\int_{F_t}g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy)=1$$
for every state $x\in E_t$ and measurable $B\subseteq F_t$. For
$h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$, let $\pi_{t-1}$ be the filtering kernel at time
$t-1$ from
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] when $t>1$, and for $t=1$ let $\pi_0$ be
the initial kernel $\mu_0$ on the singleton empty-history space. For
$A\in\mathcal E_t$, define the predictive kernel
$$\widehat\pi_t(h,A):=\int_{E_{t-1}}K_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(h,dx),$$
the evidence density
$$z_t(h,y):=\int_{E_t}g_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx),$$
and for $h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$, $y\in F_t$, and $A\in\mathcal E_t$ define
the update
$$\pi_t(h,y,A):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ag_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)}{z_t(h,y)},&0<z_t(h,y)<\infty,\\[6pt]\widehat\pi_t(h,A),&z_t(h,y)=0\text{ or }z_t(h,y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Then $\widehat\pi_t$ is a predictive kernel for $X_t$ given $Y_{1:t-1}$,
and $\pi_t$ is a filtering kernel for $X_t$ given $Y_{1:t}$. For each fixed
history $h$, the observation marginal under the conditional version
determined by $\widehat\pi_t(h,\cdot)$ has density
$z_t(h,\cdot)$ with respect to $\nu_t$ and assigns zero mass to both
$\{y:z_t(h,y)=0\}$ and $\{y:z_t(h,y)=\infty\}$. Thus the formula never
divides by zero or infinity; values on those fibers are conditional-law
fillers. The statement is exact and finite-horizon and gives no numerical
approximation or long-time stability claim.

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, standard-Borel spaces
$E_0,\ldots,E_T$ and $F_1,\ldots,F_T$, an initial probability measure
$\mu_0$ on $E_0$, and transition and observation probability kernels
$K_t:E_{t-1}\to E_t$ and $G_t:E_t\to F_t$ for $1\le t\le T$, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. On the interleaved finite
product space
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
there is a unique probability measure whose rectangle probabilities are the
ordered iterated kernel integrals
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order.
For $T=0$, the assertion is the initial law $\mu_0$ on $E_0$.

Assume AC and a finite-horizon state-space model by standard-Borel state and
observation spaces, an initial probability measure, and transition and
observation probability kernels, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. Let $P_T$ be its finite-horizon
path law. The initial filtering kernel is $\pi_0=\mu_0$ on the singleton
empty-history space. For each $1\le t\le T$, data-indexed filtering and
predictive kernels from [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] exist. A
data-indexed finite-horizon smoothing kernel for the full state path also
exists, including when $T=0$. The claim is existence of conditional versions
only; it asserts no density, filtering recursion, uniqueness on null
observation histories, or numerical approximation.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. For
$0\le t\le T$, let
$(E_t,\mathcal E_t)$ be a standard-Borel state space; for $1\le t\le T$, let
$(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ be a standard-Borel observation space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]), meaning a measurable space bimeasurably
isomorphic to a Polish space. A probability kernel has probability-measure
sections and measurable evaluations as in
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Specify an initial probability
measure $\mu_0$ on $E_0$ (a measure of total mass one, as in
[[def-probability-measure]]), transition probability kernels $K_t$ from
$E_{t-1}$ to $E_t$, and observation probability kernels $G_t$ from $E_t$ to
$F_t$, for $1\le t\le T$.

The trajectory space, with the finite product sigma-algebra generated by
measurable coordinate rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), is
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
with $\mathcal Z_0=E_0$. Its finite-horizon law $P_T$ is the unique probability
law whose ordered iterated kernel integral is
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order; it
does not assert the existence of densities. Existence and uniqueness under AC
are proved in [[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]].
Every finite product trajectory space is standard Borel by
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].

The initial and transition laws specify the state evolution, while each
$G_t$ specifies the observation law given the current state in this model.
State evolution by itself therefore does not specify a joint state-observation
law. No density or time-homogeneity assumption is imposed, and no strict
stationarity assumption (shift invariance of all finite-dimensional laws) is
required ([[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]]). This is a
single law, not a parameter-indexed family. The model contract records a
proposed law and makes no claim that it adequately describes an application
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).

Assume AC and a finite-horizon model as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. For each $1\le t\le T$, suppose
the observation kernel has a supplied product-measurable density
$g_t:E_t\times F_t\to[0,\infty]$ with respect to a sigma-finite measure
$\nu_t$ on $F_t$, normalized so that
$$G_t(x,B)=\int_Bg_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy),\qquad\int_{F_t}g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy)=1$$
for every state $x$ and measurable $B\subseteq F_t$.

The procedure takes the initial law $\mu_0$, transition kernels $K_t$,
observation densities $g_t$ and measures $\nu_t$ as inputs. It defines
data-indexed prediction, evidence, and filtering functions on every
observation history as follows.

1. Initialize $\pi_0$ on the singleton empty-history space by
$\pi_0(*,A)=\mu_0(A)$.

2. For $t=1,\ldots,T$, each history $h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$ and each
measurable state set $A\in\mathcal E_t$, form the predictive measure
$$\widehat\pi_t(h,A):=\int_{E_{t-1}}K_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(h,dx).$$

3. For each $y\in F_t$, calculate the evidence density
$$z_t(h,y):=\int_{E_t}g_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx).$$

4. Define the filtering measure at $(h,y)$ by
$$\pi_t(h,y,A):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ag_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)}{z_t(h,y)},&0<z_t(h,y)<\infty,\\[6pt]\widehat\pi_t(h,A),&z_t(h,y)=0\text{ or }z_t(h,y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Use $\pi_t$ as the input filtering function at the next time step.

The procedure returns $\widehat\pi_t$, $z_t$, and $\pi_t$ for every
$1\le t\le T$. It is an exact measure-valued recursion; it makes no claim
that the integrals have closed forms or can be evaluated with finite
computational cost. [[thm-dominated-state-space-filtering-recursion]] proves
that the returned functions are predictive and filtering kernels for the
specified finite-horizon model.

derivations.claim: Let $g_t(i,j):=G_t(i,\{j\})$ for $i,j\in\{0,1\}$. Counting measure integrates by finite sums, so $\sum_jg_t(i,j)=G_t(i,\{0,1\})=1$ and $G_t(i,C)=\sum_{j\in C}g_t(i,j)$; every function on these finite discrete spaces is product-measurable. Thus [F2] applies. Since $\mu_0$ is uniform and each transition-matrix column sums to one, $X_1$ is uniform; hence $P(Y_1=1)=\frac12(\frac14+\frac34)=\frac12$, and Bayes' finite sum gives $P(X_1=0\mid Y_1=1)=\frac{(1/2)(1/4)}{1/2}=1/4$ and $P(X_1=1\mid Y_1=1)=3/4$.

By the ordered path law [F3], for $i=0,1$ the conditional probability of $Y_2=0$ given $X_1=i,Y_1=1$ is $\sum_{j=0}^1M_{ij}G_2(j,\{0\})$; the factor $G_1(i,\{1\})$ cancels in this conditional probability because it depends only on the fixed state $i$ and event $Y_1=1$. These sums are $(3/4)(3/4)+(1/4)(1/4)=5/8$ for $i=0$ and $(1/4)(3/4)+(3/4)(1/4)=3/8$ for $i=1$. Multiplying by the time-1 filter $(1/4,3/4)$ gives conditional smoothing masses $(5/32,9/32)$; their sum is $7/16$, the conditional evidence in step 3.1, so the smoothing law of $X_1$ is $(5/14,9/14)$. The history event has positive probability by step 1.1 and step 3.1, so its conditional distribution is fixed by the event identities.

Let $n\ge 1$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and let $a\in\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). The **translate** of $E$ by $a$ is

$$E+a:=\{x+a:x\in E\}.$$

Translation by $a$ is the bijection $\tau_a(x)=x+a$, whose inverse is $\tau_{-a}$. In particular, $\varnothing+a=\varnothing$.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

([[def-countable-choice]]), let $c$ be a nonzero real and write
$cE := \{\, cx : x \in E \,\}$ for $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, where
$(cx)_i := cx_i$. Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\,\lambda_n^*(E)$ for every subset $E$, the

2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $cE$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

Assume AC and a finite-horizon model as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. For each $1\le t\le T$, let
$\nu_t$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ and suppose the
observation kernel has a specified product-measurable density
$g_t:E_t\times F_t\to[0,\infty]$ with respect to $\mathcal E_t\otimes\mathcal F_t$:
$$G_t(x,B)=\int_B g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy),\qquad\int_{F_t}g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy)=1$$
for every state $x\in E_t$ and measurable $B\subseteq F_t$. For
$h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$, let $\pi_{t-1}$ be the filtering kernel at time
$t-1$ from
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] when $t>1$, and for $t=1$ let $\pi_0$ be
the initial kernel $\mu_0$ on the singleton empty-history space. For
$A\in\mathcal E_t$, define the predictive kernel
$$\widehat\pi_t(h,A):=\int_{E_{t-1}}K_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(h,dx),$$
the evidence density
$$z_t(h,y):=\int_{E_t}g_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx),$$

$z_t(h,\cdot)$ with respect to $\nu_t$ and assigns zero mass to both
$\{y:z_t(h,y)=0\}$ and $\{y:z_t(h,y)=\infty\}$. Thus the formula never
divides by zero or infinity; values on those fibers are conditional-law
fillers. The statement is exact and finite-horizon and gives no numerical
approximation or long-time stability claim.

derivations.claim: With counting measure on $F_1$, set $g_1(x,y)=G_1(x,\{y\})$; it is jointly measurable on the finite discrete spaces, sums to one over $y$, and gives $G_1(x,C)=\sum_{y\in C}g_1(x,y)$. The factorized law [F3] gives $P(Y_1=b)=0$.

Let $\rho$ be any probability measure on $E_1$ and define $q(a,\cdot)=\delta_0$ and $q(b,\cdot)=\rho$. This is a measurable probability kernel because the observation space is finite discrete. For every $A\subseteq\{0,1\}$ and $C\subseteq\{a,b\}$, the path law gives $P(X_1\in A,Y_1\in C)=\mathbf1_A(0)\mathbf1_C(a)$, while $E[\mathbf1_{\{Y_1\in C\}}q(Y_1,A)]=\mathbf1_C(a)\delta_0(A)+0\cdot\mathbf1_C(b)\rho(A)=\mathbf1_A(0)\mathbf1_C(a)$.
